name: Picture superiority effect
statement: Material studied as pictures is remembered better than the same material studied as words, on free recall and on recognition tests alike.
meaning: The claim compares two study formats against one memory test. Participants see a list of items, some as pictures and some as printed words, and are later asked to recognise or recall them. Pictures win on both tests, and the size of the win depends on which test is used and on what the test cue looks like. Recognition asks whether an item was on the list, and performance there runs close to ceiling for pictures, which limits what a recognition comparison can show. Free recall asks the participant to produce the items unprompted, and the picture advantage is real but the absolute numbers are far lower. Two families of explanation have competed since the 1970s. Dual coding, from Allan Paivio, holds that a picture is stored twice, as an image and as a name, while a word usually gets only a verbal code. Distinctiveness accounts hold that pictures simply differ from one another more than words do, so each one is encoded more uniquely. The distinctiveness camp is itself split, between accounts resting on physical variability and accounts resting on conceptual variability. Isolation within a list is entry 111 and bizarre material is entry 252, and both turn on the same idea that an item unlike its neighbours is remembered better.

origin.note: The paper is titled 'Picture superiority in free recall: Imagery or dual coding?' and it put the name and the dual-coding explanation into the same title. Its design and result are described by McBride and Dosher: participants studied pictures, concrete words and abstract words under incidental or intentional instructions, and free recall was higher for pictures than for either kind of word. The demonstrations came earlier. Standing reports that Shepard in 1967 extended a 1965 study by Nickerson. The other name for the effect comes from the title of Nelson, Reed and Walling's 1976 paper, which is simply 'Pictorial superiority effect'.

evidence: Standing's 1973 paper is the one everybody cites and almost nobody reads. Subjects saw a single pass of slides at 5 seconds each and then took a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test. The interval was two days, except in the 4,000 and 10,000 item conditions, where the learning was spread over several days and two days is an average. With 10,000 normal pictures and 160 test trials the mean error count was 27.2, and Standing's guessing-corrected estimate is 6,600 pictures retained. Words topped out at a learning set of 1,000, where the same correction gives 615 retained, which Standing prints as 62%. Vivid pictures were run only as far as 1,000 items, and beat normal pictures at each of the six set sizes where both were used. Each cell of that table rests on five subjects, ten for vivid pictures. Standing also tested recall. Ten subjects studied 200 items and then wrote down everything they could for 40 minutes: 51.6 pictures recalled against 24.5 visually presented words, 37.5 spoken words and 11.25 nonsense syllables. Forty recognition trials on the same 200 items gave estimates of 175 pictures against 134.5 visual words. The often-quoted 98% is Shepard's, not Standing's, and it is a different design. Standing describes it as one exposure of 612 pictures at about 6 seconds each, after which subjects picked the old item in two-alternative tests with 98% success, against 90% for single words and 88% for short sentences. Ensor, Surprenant and Neath describe the same study as 612 colour pictures and 540 words, with 96.7% correct for pictures and 88.4% for words. Shepard's own paper could not be read here, so the two second-hand accounts stand unreconciled. Cherry and colleagues ran the largest modern test located here. They gave 160 adults in four age bands a list of pictures and matching words, scored free recall as a proportion of 16 items, and found 0.52 for pictures against 0.36 for words, F(1, 156) = 117.91, p < 0.001. Corrected recognition was 0.94 against 0.80, F(1, 156) = 112.88, p < 0.0001.

examples.tag: The diagram beside the fire door
examples.text: A notice describes the route to the exit in three sentences. The same route drawn as a floor plan with an arrow is what people can reproduce a week later, from the same few seconds of attention.

A presentation makes one point in a line of text and the next in a single image. Weeks later the audience can say what the picture showed and not what the line said, although both were on screen for the same time.
Ten items sketched as small pictures are recalled more completely than the same ten written out as words. The items are identical and the only difference is the form they were studied in.

replication.headline: The effect reproduces across the adult lifespan and in patients with Alzheimer's disease, though the reason for it is still argued over.
replication.detail: Cherry, Hawley, Jackson, Volaufova, Su and Jazwinski tested 40 middle-aged adults (mean 51.7 years), 40 young-old (69.7), 40 old-old (80.5) and 40 oldest-old (92.4). Pictures beat words on free recall, 0.52 against 0.36, F(1, 156) = 117.91, MSE = 0.02, p < 0.001, and the age group by stimulus format interaction was not significant, so every band showed a pictorial advantage of similar size. On corrected recognition the means were 0.94 for pictures and 0.80 for words, F(1, 156) = 112.88, MSE = 0.01, p < 0.0001, and here the interaction was reliable, F(3, 156) = 6.49, p < 0.001, with the oldest-old gaining most. The authors warn that the three younger groups were near ceiling, which limits what that second interaction can mean. The same group repeated the work in 2012 on a fresh sample of 160, and recall was again higher for pictures, 0.55 against 0.43, F(1, 154) = 69.77, p < 0.001, with recognition 0.92 against 0.76, F(1, 154) = 114.79, p < 0.0001. An earlier aging study by Winograd, Smith and Simon had found the advantage in younger but not older subjects in its first experiment, then found it in both groups with no age interaction in two further experiments. Ally, Gold and Budson tested recognition memory in 18 healthy older adults, 17 patients with mild cognitive impairment and 19 with Alzheimer's disease. On the discrimination index the effect of picture over word study was F(1, 50) = 18.6, p < 0.001, and the group by format interaction did not reach significance, F(2, 50) = 1.94, p = 0.154, which is the basis for saying the patients gained as much as the controls. That is a null result on 54 people and it bounds how similar the benefit can be said to be.

study.cite: Cherry, K. E., Hawley, K. S., Jackson, E. M., Volaufova, J., Su, L. J., & Jazwinski, S. M. (2008). Pictorial superiority effects in oldest-old people. Memory, 16(7), 728-741.

limits: Change the test and the effect changes sign. Weldon and Roediger gave 90 Purdue undergraduates a mixed list of pictures and words, and then both a free recall test and a word-fragment completion test, with the order counterbalanced. Free recall showed the usual pattern, 0.39 for pictures against 0.29 for words, F(1, 88) = 28.31. Priming on fragment completion ran the other way, 0.26 for words against 0.11 for pictures, F(1, 88) = 48.59. Pictures did prime word fragments a little, 7% when that test came first, t(44) = 2.21, p < 0.05, which the authors did not expect. In their fourth experiment 90 further students took either word-fragment completion or picture-fragment identification, and word superiority held on the first while pictures won on the second. McBride and Dosher tabulate seventeen results from five papers: picture superiority on explicit free recall, semantic cued recall and category production and on implicit picture-fragment identification, word superiority on word-fragment and word-stem completion, and no difference at all on implicit category production and word association. The advantage follows the match between how an item was studied and what the test cue looks like, not the item's format alone. Whether equating encoding shrinks it is disputed. McBride and Dosher note that under a semantic study instruction such as rating pleasantness, Paivio found recall for words and pictures similar. Two aging studies run the other way. Winograd, Smith and Simon report that a semantic orienting task had no effect on recall, and Cherry and colleagues in 2012 found the advantage larger after semantic orienting than after standard instructions, F(1, 154) = 9.42, p = 0.003, with the orienting task raising picture recall and leaving word recall alone. Nelson, Reed and Walling manipulated visual similarity among the pictures in a paired-associate task, and report that high similarity removed the advantage at the slow presentation rate and reversed it at the fast one. Standing's capacity figures rest on five subjects per cell and a single laboratory, and his estimate that a million vivid pictures would yield 731,400 retained is an extrapolation from a fitted line, not a measurement. No meta-analysis of the picture superiority effect was located. Crossref bibliographic queries, OpenAlex, PubMed and Semantic Scholar were tried on 21 September 2026, and the only meta-analysis returned was Schubbe and colleagues on pictures in health communication, which is not a test of this effect. No test of the effect in a non-Western sample was located by those same searches, so nothing here supports or denies that it is universal.
misreadings: The retention pyramid attached to this effect in training decks is invented. The chart claiming people remember 10% of what they read, 20% of what they hear and 30% of what they see is not Edgar Dale's, who put no numbers on his cone, and it carries no study behind it. Letrud and Hernes searched digital libraries and found versions of the pyramid in educational debate for more than 160 years, concluding that the models did not come from empirical research and that the account of memory they imply departs from the standard one. Subramony, Molenda, Betrus and Thalheimer published four articles on its history in Educational Technology in 2014, listed by the Debunker Club, which were not obtained for this entry. The single most repeated applied figure is also unsourced. John Medina's Brain Rules blog states that people remember about 10 percent of orally presented information 72 hours later, and that the figure goes up to 65 percent if a picture is added. That post carries no citation for either number, and no document giving them was located. The second error is treating Shepard's 98% as a claim about memory in general. It is two-alternative forced choice, where a coin scores 50, and it says nothing about whether anyone could describe those 612 pictures. Recall of the same material sits far lower: 51.6 items out of 200 in Standing's recall experiment. The third error is treating dual coding as settled. Ensor, Surprenant and Neath raised the physical distinctiveness of words with varied fonts, sizes, colours and capitalisation and lowered that of pictures by using black-and-white line drawings. Against black words, black-and-white pictures kept their advantage. Against distinctive words they lost it, d' of 2.959 against 2.969 in the first experiment, t(29) = 0.056, and 1.896 against 1.885 in the second. In a third experiment, which also made the pictures share a horizontal outline, the distinctive words beat the pictures outright, 2.963 against 2.286, t(29) = 3.280, p < 0.01. Higdon, Neath, Surprenant and Ensor extended that to associative recognition and free recall and argue dual coding is no longer viable. Ensor, this time with Bancroft and Hockley, failed across four experiments to find an auditory analogue in recognition, although one exists in free recall, and proposed that dual coding underpins the free-recall version while conceptual distinctiveness underpins the recognition version. Yan, Roberts and Bainbridge tested people with aphantasia, who cannot summon voluntary mental imagery and so should gain nothing from a second visual code, and report that the picture advantage survived in them. The last error is the advertising one. Childers and Houston found picture superiority in consumer memory conditional on how the ad was processed, present at both immediate and delayed recall when processing was directed at appearance, and absent at immediate recall but back at delayed recall when it was directed at meaning.
